item.title: Building a Privacy-Preserving AI Assistant for Meshtastic
item.category: "Network Security" , "Privacy" , "Open Source" , "Automation"
item.description: A practical account of building a local AI assistant for Meshtastic, with private configuration, queued TCP access, retrieval tools, and a safer dashboard.
item.content:encoded: <p>Meshtastic provides text communication over low-power LoRa radios. Ollama provides a way to run an open model on local hardware. I combined the two into a small assistant that answers messages over a private mesh setup.</p> <h2 id="why-build-this"> <a href="#why-build-this" title="Why build this?">Why build this?</a> <a href="#why-build-this" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why build this?">#</a> </h2> <p>The goal was not to put a chatbot on a radio for its own sake. The goal was to make useful information available when normal internet services are unavailable, undesirable, or too dependent on a cloud account. A local assistant can keep questions, retrieved context, and responses inside the deployment while still using the mesh as a low-bandwidth interface.</p> <p>Power was part of that design goal. A useful node should be small enough to run on a Raspberry Pi 4, and efficient enough that a future deployment could pair it with a battery and a solar panel. Solar operation is an engineering target rather than a guaranteed property: the model, storage, radio, display, battery, panel, weather, and duty cycle all affect the energy budget. The practical design principle is to keep the services local, the answers concise, and the hardware modest so an off-grid version remains plausible.</p> <p>The project started as a simple Python bridge. It grew into a service with message filtering, source retrieval, a local control API, and a dashboard. The most useful lessons came from the failures. Each failure forced a clearer boundary between the radio connection, the model, and the web interface.</p> <h2 id="the-first-version-was-deliberately-small"> <a href="#the-first-version-was-deliberately-small" title="The first version was deliberately small">The first version was deliberately small</a> <a href="#the-first-version-was-deliberately-small" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The first version was deliberately small">#</a> </h2> <p>The first design had four parts:</p> <ul> <li>A Meshtastic node handled radio traffic.</li> <li>A Python process listened for text packets.</li> <li>Ollama generated a response on local hardware.</li> <li>The bridge sent the response back to the sender.</li> </ul> <p>The bridge used an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint. This kept the model interface simple and left the model choice in an environment file.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Meshtastic node -> TCP -> Python bridge -> local model </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> | </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> reply over Meshtastic </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The assistant answered direct messages first. This reduced noise while the message path was being tested.</p> <h2 id="channel-messages-needed-an-explicit-trigger"> <a href="#channel-messages-needed-an-explicit-trigger" title="Channel messages needed an explicit trigger">Channel messages needed an explicit trigger</a> <a href="#channel-messages-needed-an-explicit-trigger" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Channel messages needed an explicit trigger">#</a> </h2> <p>Answering every broadcast message would create noise and consume radio airtime. The bridge now ignores ordinary channel traffic. A channel request must start with a configurable prefix.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot what is a checksum? </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot weather <city or postal code> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot news <topic> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot wiki <subject> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Direct messages do not need the prefix. The prefix rule keeps the assistant quiet during normal mesh conversations.</p> <p>The prefix lives in the private environment file:</p> <pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-dotenv" data-lang="dotenv">REPLY_TO_BROADCAST=true BOT_PREFIX=!bot </code></pre><h2 id="the-tcp-connection-became-the-main-design-problem"> <a href="#the-tcp-connection-became-the-main-design-problem" title="The TCP connection became the main design problem">The TCP connection became the main design problem</a> <a href="#the-tcp-connection-became-the-main-design-problem" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The TCP connection became the main design problem">#</a> </h2> <p>The Meshtastic node accepts one active client for its TCP API in this setup. The bridge owned the connection. The dashboard also tried to run the Meshtastic command-line client for status pages. Those two clients competed for the same socket.</p> <p>The result was confusing. The bridge process stayed active, yet its reader thread had stopped. A dashboard refresh was able to disconnect message handling. A node reconnect left a stale process behind.</p> <p>The fix was to make the bridge the only TCP owner.</p> <p>The bridge now exposes a small control API on the local machine. The dashboard asks the bridge for status, node data, and channel data. It never opens a second Meshtastic connection.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Dashboard -> local control API -> queued bridge operation -> Meshtastic TCP node </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> ^ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Meshtastic TCP connection owned by the bridge </span></span></code></pre></div><p>A queue serializes control requests. A lock protects writes shared by the dashboard operations and bot replies. A heartbeat keeps idle TCP sessions open. A connection watchdog lets the service manager restart the bridge after a disconnect.</p> <p>This design also improves diagnosis. The dashboard reports connection state and queue depth without touching the radio session.</p> <h2 id="local-inference-required-practical-limits"> <a href="#local-inference-required-practical-limits" title="Local inference required practical limits">Local inference required practical limits</a> <a href="#local-inference-required-practical-limits" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Local inference required practical limits">#</a> </h2> <p>The target hardware has limited memory. The first model choice was too large for comfortable use. Prompt length, model loading, and radio-sized replies all affected response time.</p> <p>The final setup uses a smaller local model and a short reply limit. The bridge splits longer responses into multiple Meshtastic packets. The system also uses compressed memory swap and a conservative CPU setting on the host.</p> <p>These settings are not substitutes for a larger computer. They reduce avoidable pressure while keeping the service local.</p> <h2 id="retrieval-belongs-outside-the-system-prompt"> <a href="#retrieval-belongs-outside-the-system-prompt" title="Retrieval belongs outside the system prompt">Retrieval belongs outside the system prompt</a> <a href="#retrieval-belongs-outside-the-system-prompt" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Retrieval belongs outside the system prompt">#</a> </h2> <p>A small language model does not provide current weather or current news from its weights. The bridge added short, on-demand retrieval paths instead of downloading a full encyclopedia to the device.</p> <p>Supported requests include:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Wikipedia</strong> retrieves a matching page summary.</li> <li><strong>Weather</strong> retrieves a short current-condition line.</li> <li><strong>News</strong> reads recent titles from an RSS search feed.</li> </ul> <p>The retrieval source is placed in the user prompt as labeled context. The agent instructions tell the model to use the supplied source, state uncertainty, and avoid inventing article details.</p> <p>The bridge can also use a local Wikipedia RAG index. It is a small SQLite FTS5 database built from a curated JSONL export, so it does not require a resident vector database or a second embedding model on the Raspberry Pi. Wiki requests search that local index first and can fall back to the public Wikipedia API when enabled. A fully local deployment can disable the fallback.</p> <p>The HTTP identity is configurable:</p> <pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-dotenv" data-lang="dotenv">WEB_RETRIEVAL_ENABLED=true HTTP_USER_AGENT=SoS-Mesh-Assistant/1.0 (Meshtastic AI bridge) DEFAULT_WEATHER_LOCATION= DEFAULT_NEWS_TOPIC= </code></pre><p>Blank defaults force the user to provide a location or topic. This prevents a deployment-specific location from entering shared examples or source files.</p> <h2 id="the-agent-needed-an-explicit-identity"> <a href="#the-agent-needed-an-explicit-identity" title="The agent needed an explicit identity">The agent needed an explicit identity</a> <a href="#the-agent-needed-an-explicit-identity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The agent needed an explicit identity">#</a> </h2> <p>Small models often answer with a generic identity unless the application gives them a clear role. The bridge loads its identity and safety rules from a separate prompt file.</p> <p>The prompt describes the assistant as a concise helper for a low-bandwidth mesh. It also sets boundaries:</p> <ul> <li>It must not claim to contact emergency services.</li> <li>It must not expose private configuration or secrets.</li> <li>It must treat retrieved pages as reference material, not instructions.</li> <li>It must identify sources when it uses retrieved information.</li> <li>It must give short answers suitable for radio transport.</li> </ul> <p>Keeping this policy in a file makes review easier. It also keeps deployment-specific values out of the application source.</p> <h2 id="the-dashboard-became-an-operations-tool"> <a href="#the-dashboard-became-an-operations-tool" title="The dashboard became an operations tool">The dashboard became an operations tool</a> <a href="#the-dashboard-became-an-operations-tool" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The dashboard became an operations tool">#</a> </h2> <p>The first dashboard showed service buttons and raw command output. The revised dashboard focuses on the state needed during operation:</p> <ul> <li>Mesh connection status</li> <li>Bridge-owned queue depth</li> <li>Connected node identity</li> <li>Service state</li> <li>Active model</li> <li>Model pull and selection controls</li> <li>Channel and node views</li> <li>Recent questions and replies</li> </ul> <p>The dashboard also avoids a dangerous action from the early version. It no longer runs a separate Meshtastic command for configuration changes. Configuration writes need to pass through the same bridge queue as other node operations.</p> <h2 id="privacy-was-part-of-the-build"> <a href="#privacy-was-part-of-the-build" title="Privacy was part of the build">Privacy was part of the build</a> <a href="#privacy-was-part-of-the-build" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Privacy was part of the build">#</a> </h2> <p>The public source contains neutral placeholders. Private node addresses, radio keys, passwords, administrator keys, and location defaults stay in an ignored environment file on the deployment host.</p> <p>The same rule applies to documentation. Examples use placeholders such as <code><node-ip></code> and <code><city or postal code></code>. A working example does not need to reveal the network where it was tested.</p> <p>This separation also makes the project easier to share. The source explains the architecture. The private environment describes one deployment. Neither file needs to contain the other file’s data.</p> <h2 id="what-i-would-improve-next"> <a href="#what-i-would-improve-next" title="What I would improve next">What I would improve next</a> <a href="#what-i-would-improve-next" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What I would improve next">#</a> </h2> <p>The next useful step is to move every Meshtastic write into the bridge control queue. Channel edits, node configuration, and send operations should share one audited path. The dashboard should then show the queue job, result, and error message for each operation.</p> <p>The current build already demonstrates the core pattern. Keep one owner for the radio connection, keep deployment values outside source control, and pass external information to the model as labeled context. The longer-term ideal is a quiet, low-power node that can continue providing local knowledge and mesh assistance from a Raspberry Pi 4, including during a solar-powered deployment.</p> <h2 id="define-the-off-grid-acceptance-test"> <a href="#define-the-off-grid-acceptance-test" title="Define the off-grid acceptance test">Define the off-grid acceptance test</a> <a href="#define-the-off-grid-acceptance-test" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Define the off-grid acceptance test">#</a> </h2> <p>Treat solar operation as a measured operating mode. Log radio uptime, queue depth, model load time, reply length, battery voltage, and retrieval failures during the same test window. Then set a clear fallback, such as local answers only, queued replies, or an explicit unavailable response when energy or network conditions cross your limit.</p> <p>The privacy boundary also needs a failure test. Disable external retrieval, inspect application logs, and confirm the bridge still answers local questions without sending private configuration to a remote service. Test the dashboard from the administration network only, and keep the radio queue as the single owner of node writes.</p> <p>Meshtastic documentation: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Meshtastic introduction"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://meshtastic.org/docs/"> <a href="https://meshtastic.org/docs/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Meshtastic introduction</a> </span> </p> <p>Local model runtime: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Ollama"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/"> <a href="https://ollama.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Ollama</a> </span> </p> <p>Wikipedia API reference: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Wikipedia REST API page summary"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/summary/Wikipedia"> <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/summary/Wikipedia" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Wikipedia REST API page summary</a> </span> </p> <p>Source code: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Meshtastic AI Bridge on GitHub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/meshtastic-ai-bridge"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/meshtastic-ai-bridge" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Meshtastic AI Bridge on GitHub</a> </span> </p> Read More at https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: SenseCAP M1 Raspberry Pi Shield: Pinout and LoRaWAN Reuse
item.category: "Raspberry Pi" , "IoT" , "Hardware Security"
item.description: Understand the SenseCAP M1 shield, compare conflicting GPIO maps, inspect its ATECC608, and plan a LoRaWAN gateway with modern Raspberry Pi OS.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>The SenseCAP M1 shield is useful LoRaWAN gateway hardware, but its wiring deserves more scrutiny than a generic Raspberry Pi HAT tutorial provides.</strong> This guide expands <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Clockwork Bird’s 2023 investigation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/"> <a href="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Clockwork Bird’s 2023 investigation</a> </span> with manufacturer documentation, upstream driver inspection, and current GPIO guidance. You will identify the hardware, separate established facts from incomplete pinout evidence, and produce a repeatable bring-up record.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Scope:</strong> This is a documentation-based hardware guide. The commands and board mappings have not been tested on a physical M1 for this article.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="要点"> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" title="要点">要点</a> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="要点">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Identify both boards:</strong> The M1 carrier and its removable concentrator have separate model and revision information.</li> <li><strong>Audit reset scripts:</strong> CoreCell defaults conflict with signals in the published M1 pinout.</li> <li><strong>Check the OS interfaces:</strong> SPI device files, GPIO numbering, and GPIO tool versions answer different questions.</li> <li><strong>Preserve secure-element provisioning:</strong> Reading device information differs from configuring or generating keys.</li> <li><strong>Prove the whole path:</strong> A detected concentrator does not establish successful sensor delivery.</li> </ul> <h2 id="开始之前"> <a href="#%e5%bc%80%e5%a7%8b%e4%b9%8b%e5%89%8d" title="开始之前">开始之前</a> <a href="#%e5%bc%80%e5%a7%8b%e4%b9%8b%e5%89%8d" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="开始之前">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Difficulty: intermediate.</strong> Budget roughly one to two hours for inventory, OS preparation, and documentation checks. Electrical verification, driver adaptation, and network-server deployment add separate work, especially with an unfamiliar board revision.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Item</th> <th>Purpose</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>M1 shield and concentrator</strong></td> <td>Read the carrier revision and the complete module label</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Raspberry Pi 4</strong></td> <td>Start with the host used in the original M1 design</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Spare microSD card</strong></td> <td>Prepare a separate OS while preserving the original installation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Correct supply and antenna</strong></td> <td>Match the assembled hardware and the module’s RF band</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SSH or local console</strong></td> <td>Record diagnostics and edit configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>LoRaWAN sensor and server</strong></td> <td>Verify actual application delivery after hardware bring-up</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Meter and hardware experience</strong></td> <td>Resolve undocumented connections before driving them</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Photograph both sides of your unpowered assembly before removing anything. Record connector orientation, screws, spacers, and antenna routing. Keep the original card and configuration available until the replacement installation passes your acceptance checks.</p> <h2 id="identify-the-three-layers"> <a href="#identify-the-three-layers" title="Identify the Three Layers">Identify the Three Layers</a> <a href="#identify-the-three-layers" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Identify the Three Layers">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The complete M1, its carrier shield, and its concentrator are different components.</strong> Seeed documents the assembled hotspot as a Raspberry Pi 4 with either a WM1302/SX1302 or WM1303/SX1303 concentrator. A listing titled “SenseCAP M1 shield” does not establish which of those parts accompanies the carrier. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Seeed Studio’s M1 overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.sensecapmx.com/docs/sensecap-m1/overview/"> <a href="https://www.sensecapmx.com/docs/sensecap-m1/overview/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Seeed Studio’s M1 overview</a> </span> </p> <p>The <strong>carrier</strong> routes power and peripheral signals between the Pi and module. The <strong>concentrator</strong> handles radio reception and transmission. A <strong>packet forwarder</strong> runs on the host and exchanges received radio packets and scheduled downlinks with a server. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Semtech’s SX1302 HAL overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal"> <a href="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Semtech’s SX1302 HAL overview</a> </span> </p> <p>For a practical example, a shelf-temperature sensor sends an uplink over radio. The concentrator receives it, the host forwards it, and the network/application services process it. A successful Linux boot proves only the host portion of this chain.</p> <p>Clockwork Bird’s photograph shows an M1 v1.1 carrier with a module explicitly labeled <code>WM1302-SPI-EU868</code>. Use the photograph to locate the labels on your own hardware. Its serial numbers identify the photographed equipment, not configuration values for another gateway.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/m1-carrier-wm1302-board.webp", "caption": "Green M1 carrier holding a labeled WM1302 SPI EU868 module beside USB-C, button, fan socket, and antenna cable", "creditText": "Clockwork Bird", "isBasedOn": "https:\/\/clockworkbird9.wordpress.com\/2023\/05\/03\/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield\/", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-11-08 22:11:32.582978982 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b74.414758107", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-11-08 22:11:32.582978982 +0000 UTC m=+74.414758107"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="creditText" content="Clockwork Bird"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/m1-carrier-wm1302-board.webp" alt="Green M1 carrier holding a labeled WM1302 SPI EU868 module beside USB-C, button, fan socket, and antenna cable"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>M1 v1.1 hardware photographed by Clockwork Bird, also used for this article’s cover · <a href="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/">Clockwork Bird, 2023-05-03</a></p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="power-and-radio-connections"> <a href="#power-and-radio-connections" title="Power and Radio Connections">Power and Radio Connections</a> <a href="#power-and-radio-connections" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Power and Radio Connections">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Treat the M1 USB-C connector as a power input.</strong> The manufacturer specifies DC 5 V, 3 A for the complete gateway and identifies USB-C as its power-supply interface. Calling it a charging port suggests a battery function absent from those specifications. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SenseCAP M1 specifications"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.sensecapmx.com/docs/sensecap-m1/overview/"> <a href="https://www.sensecapmx.com/docs/sensecap-m1/overview/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >SenseCAP M1 specifications</a> </span> </p> <p>The vendor block diagram separates the 5 V supply from the module’s regulated 3.3 V rail. This distinction matters during troubleshooting: a running Pi and an unpowered concentrator are separate possibilities. Do not inject 5 V into a signal pin or assume two power inputs are isolated from each other.</p> <p><strong>SPI and USB module variants require different host connections.</strong> Seeed’s WM1302 documentation describes direct SPI access for its SPI model and an STM32L4 USB bridge for its USB model. The mini-PCIe shape describes the module’s form factor, while the documented electrical interfaces are SPI or USB. A matching laptop socket is insufficient evidence of compatibility. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Seeed’s WM1302 documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/seeed-lora/WM1302-doc"> <a href="https://github.com/seeed-lora/WM1302-doc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Seeed’s WM1302 documentation</a> </span> </p> <p>Before powering the assembly, seat the module with power disconnected and attach a suitable antenna. Match the RF hardware, antenna, and intended network plan. Changing a configuration filename does not replace the module’s RF components, and the M1 power socket does not prove support for a USB concentrator variant.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/m1-power-spi-system-diagram.webp", "caption": "Block diagram connecting Raspberry Pi 4 to the M1 shield through power, SPI, GPIO, and I2C buses", "creditText": "Seeed Studio \/ SenseCAP, via Clockwork Bird", "isBasedOn": "https:\/\/www.sensecapmx.com\/docs\/sensecap-m1\/overview\/", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-11-08 22:11:32.583322329 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b74.415101444", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-11-08 22:11:32.583322329 +0000 UTC m=+74.415101444"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="creditText" content="Seeed Studio / SenseCAP, via Clockwork Bird"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/m1-power-spi-system-diagram.webp" alt="Block diagram connecting Raspberry Pi 4 to the M1 shield through power, SPI, GPIO, and I2C buses"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>SenseCAP manufacturer diagram reproduced in Clockwork Bird’s original article, showing the WM1302 design · <a href="https://www.sensecapmx.com/docs/sensecap-m1/overview/">Seeed Studio / SenseCAP, via Clockwork Bird</a></p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="read-the-pinout-carefully"> <a href="#read-the-pinout-carefully" title="Read the Pinout Carefully">Read the Pinout Carefully</a> <a href="#read-the-pinout-carefully" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Read the Pinout Carefully">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Use BCM GPIO numbers and physical header numbers as separate columns in your notes.</strong> For example, BCM GPIO17 sits at physical pin 11 on the Pi header. The module edge connector introduces a third numbering system, so its reset pin number is not a Raspberry Pi GPIO number.</p> <p>The table below transcribes the connections in Clockwork Bird’s annotated header image. It is a <strong>community reference</strong>, not a complete manufacturer-issued schematic or a measurement of every M1 revision. The drawing also uses <code>SX1262</code> labels, while the generic Semtech reset script uses <code>SX1261</code> names.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Signal in the drawing</th> <th>BCM / physical pin</th> <th>Interpretation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>I2C SDA / SCL</strong></td> <td>GPIO2 / 3, GPIO3 / 5</td> <td>Shared management bus</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SX1302 reset</strong></td> <td>GPIO17 / 11</td> <td>Concentrator reset candidate</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>User LED</strong></td> <td>GPIO22 / 15</td> <td>M1 annotation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SPI MOSI / MISO</strong></td> <td>GPIO10 / 19, GPIO9 / 21</td> <td>SPI data signals</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SPI clock</strong></td> <td>GPIO11 / 23</td> <td>SPI clock signal</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SX1302 chip select</strong></td> <td>GPIO8 / 24</td> <td>SPI0 CE0</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SX1262 reset</strong></td> <td>GPIO5 / 29</td> <td>Auxiliary radio reset candidate</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SX1262 chip select</strong></td> <td>GPIO6 / 31</td> <td>GPIO6, distinct from SPI0 CE1</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SX1262 BUSY</strong></td> <td>GPIO18 / 12</td> <td>Auxiliary radio status output</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SX1262 IO1 / IO2</strong></td> <td>GPIO23 / 16, GPIO24 / 18</td> <td>Auxiliary signals, verify before use</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The crossed-out GPS/UART annotations do not establish a GPS-equipped M1. Leave GPS-specific setup out of your configuration unless your actual hardware provides it. The published diagram also leaves the user button and fan control unresolved. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Clockwork Bird’s pinout investigation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/"> <a href="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Clockwork Bird’s pinout investigation</a> </span> </p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/m1-community-header-pinout.webp", "caption": "Annotated Raspberry Pi header drawing showing M1 LED, concentrator reset, SPI signals, and crossed-out GPS connections", "creditText": "Clockwork Bird", "isBasedOn": "https:\/\/clockworkbird9.wordpress.com\/2023\/05\/03\/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield\/", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-11-08 22:11:32.583558225 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b74.415337340", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-11-08 22:11:32.583558225 +0000 UTC m=+74.415337340"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="creditText" content="Clockwork Bird"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/m1-community-header-pinout.webp" alt="Annotated Raspberry Pi header drawing showing M1 LED, concentrator reset, SPI signals, and crossed-out GPS connections"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Community-annotated reference with unresolved board-revision coverage, not a complete M1 schematic · <a href="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/">Clockwork Bird, 2023-05-03</a></p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="resolve-reset-script-conflicts"> <a href="#resolve-reset-script-conflicts" title="Resolve Reset-Script Conflicts">Resolve Reset-Script Conflicts</a> <a href="#resolve-reset-script-conflicts" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Resolve Reset-Script Conflicts">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A reset script selects electrical outputs, not merely software preferences.</strong> Semtech’s upstream <code>reset_lgw.sh</code> targets its CoreCell reference design. Its defaults include GPIO23 for concentrator reset, GPIO18 for power enable, GPIO22 for auxiliary reset, and GPIO13 for an AD5338R reset. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Semtech reset-script source"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal/blob/master/tools/reset_lgw.sh"> <a href="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal/blob/master/tools/reset_lgw.sh" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Semtech reset-script source</a> </span> </p> <p>Seeed’s older setup instructions change the two reset assignments to GPIO17 and GPIO5 but retain the other reference-design entries. Compare those values with the annotated M1 image before following the example. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Seeed WM1302 setup instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/seeed-lora/WM1302-doc"> <a href="https://github.com/seeed-lora/WM1302-doc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Seeed WM1302 setup instructions</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Assignment</th> <th>Conflicting evidence</th> <th>Required decision</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>GPIO22 as auxiliary reset</strong></td> <td>M1 image labels it as the user LED</td> <td>Remove this assumption before enabling the LED</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GPIO18 as power enable</strong></td> <td>M1 image labels it as auxiliary BUSY</td> <td>Verify the net and direction before driving it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GPIO13 as DAC reset</strong></td> <td>Generic script names a different reference design</td> <td>Establish whether the circuit exists</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Auxiliary SPI device</strong></td> <td>M1 image selects GPIO6 rather than CE1</td> <td>Confirm chip-select routing and driver support</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Inference:</strong> If GPIO18 connects to an auxiliary radio output as drawn, configuring the Pi end as an output creates a risk of electrical contention. The disagreement establishes a verification requirement, not proof of damage or proof of one universal M1 wiring map.</p> <p>With all power disconnected, trace accessible connections between the header and module connector. Record the board revision and both endpoints. A continuity result establishes connectivity, while the component documentation establishes signal direction and electrical limits.</p> <p>Use the manufacturer’s module diagram below to avoid mixing edge-connector pins with Pi header pins. The auxiliary-radio labels describe the published module reference and do not establish identical silicon or supported features across every module revision. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Seeed WM1302 module pinout"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/seeed-lora/WM1302-doc/blob/master/pinout.jpg"> <a href="https://github.com/seeed-lora/WM1302-doc/blob/master/pinout.jpg" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Seeed WM1302 module pinout</a> </span> </p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/wm1302-module-edge-connector.webp", "caption": "Seeed diagram labeling both sides of the WM1302 module edge connector with power, SPI, I2C, and auxiliary radio signals", "creditText": "Seeed Studio", "isBasedOn": "https:\/\/github.com\/seeed-lora\/WM1302-doc", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-11-08 22:11:32.583764145 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b74.415543260", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/zh.simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-11-08 22:11:32.583764145 +0000 UTC m=+74.415543260"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="creditText" content="Seeed Studio"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/wm1302-module-edge-connector.webp" alt="Seeed diagram labeling both sides of the WM1302 module edge connector with power, SPI, I2C, and auxiliary radio signals"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Module edge-connector numbering differs from Raspberry Pi header numbering · <a href="https://github.com/seeed-lora/WM1302-doc">Seeed Studio, WM1302-doc</a></p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="prepare-raspberry-pi-os"> <a href="#prepare-raspberry-pi-os" title="Prepare Raspberry Pi OS">Prepare Raspberry Pi OS</a> <a href="#prepare-raspberry-pi-os" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prepare Raspberry Pi OS">#</a> </h2> <p>Record the host environment on your spare installation:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /etc/os-release </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>uname -r </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>tr -d <span style="color:#e6db74">'\0'</span> < /proc/device-tree/model </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The OS release, kernel, and Pi model form the starting point for reproducibility. Record them before comparing your results with an older tutorial.</p> <p>Install inspection and build tools:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo apt update </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo apt install git build-essential i2c-tools gpiod </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo raspi-config </span></span></code></pre></div><p>In <strong>Interface Options</strong>, enable SPI and I2C, then reboot. SPI serves the concentrator path, while I2C supports the management devices discussed below. Avoid importing unrelated GPS serial-port changes from another HAT tutorial.</p> <p>Inspect the exposed interfaces:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ls -l /dev/spidev* /dev/i2c-* </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>i2cdetect -l </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>gpiodetect </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>gpioinfo </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>gpioset --version </span></span></code></pre></div><p>These commands list device nodes, adapters, GPIO controllers, line information, and the installed GPIO tool version. <strong><code>i2cdetect -l</code> lists adapters without scanning device addresses.</strong> A <code>/dev/spidev0.0</code> file establishes an exposed SPI interface, not communication with a working concentrator. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="i2c-tools manual"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/utils/i2c-tools/i2c-tools/+/refs/tags/v4.3/tools/i2cdetect.8"> <a href="https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/utils/i2c-tools/i2c-tools/+/refs/tags/v4.3/tools/i2cdetect.8" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >i2c-tools manual</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Raspberry Pi GPIO guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/685-app-notes-guides-whitepapers/documents/RP-006553-WP/A-history-of-GPIO-usage-on-Raspberry-Pi-devices-and-current-best-practices"> <a href="https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/685-app-notes-guides-whitepapers/documents/RP-006553-WP/A-history-of-GPIO-usage-on-Raspberry-Pi-devices-and-current-best-practices" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Raspberry Pi GPIO guidance</a> </span> </p> <h3 id="account-for-gpio-versions"> <a href="#account-for-gpio-versions" title="Account for GPIO Versions">Account for GPIO Versions</a> <a href="#account-for-gpio-versions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Account for GPIO Versions">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Do not copy global GPIO numbers from another machine.</strong> Old scripts write through <code>/sys/class/gpio</code>, an interface the kernel documents as deprecated. New userspace integrations should use the GPIO character-device interface, with the correct controller and line offset. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Linux GPIO documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/next/admin-guide/gpio/sysfs.html"> <a href="https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/next/admin-guide/gpio/sysfs.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Linux GPIO documentation</a> </span> </p> <p>Also inspect <code>gpioset --help</code> before adapting a script. Version 1 and version 2 differ in syntax and process behavior. The current tool holds requested lines by default, and its portable contract does not guarantee their state after process exit. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="libgpiod gpioset documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://libgpiod.readthedocs.io/en/master/gpioset.html"> <a href="https://libgpiod.readthedocs.io/en/master/gpioset.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >libgpiod gpioset documentation</a> </span> </p> <p>Raspberry Pi documents an output-persistence behavior in its kernel, with options to change it. Record the actual kernel configuration instead of assuming every Linux system behaves identically. Neither updated numbering nor a newer GPIO tool resolves an incorrect electrical mapping. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Raspberry Pi GPIO usage guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/685-app-notes-guides-whitepapers/documents/RP-006553-WP/A-history-of-GPIO-usage-on-Raspberry-Pi-devices-and-current-best-practices"> <a href="https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/685-app-notes-guides-whitepapers/documents/RP-006553-WP/A-history-of-GPIO-usage-on-Raspberry-Pi-devices-and-current-best-practices" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Raspberry Pi GPIO usage guide</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="test-the-user-led"> <a href="#test-the-user-led" title="Test the User LED">Test the User LED</a> <a href="#test-the-user-led" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test the User LED">#</a> </h2> <p>After verifying GPIO22 belongs to the LED and removing conflicting GPIO consumers, edit the boot configuration:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudoedit /boot/firmware/config.txt </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Modern Raspberry Pi OS mounts the boot configuration at <strong><code>/boot/firmware/config.txt</code></strong>. Older images use <code>/boot/config.txt</code>, the path in the 2023 article. Back up the active file before editing it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Raspberry Pi config.txt documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/config_txt.html"> <a href="https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/config_txt.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Raspberry Pi config.txt documentation</a> </span> </p> <p>Add the LED overlay under a section applying to your Pi, such as <code>[all]</code>:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-ini" data-lang="ini"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#a6e22e">dtoverlay</span><span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">gpio-led,gpio=22,label=lorawan,trigger=heartbeat</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The <strong><code>gpio</code></strong> parameter uses BCM numbering. <strong><code>label</code></strong> names the Linux LED device, and <strong><code>trigger=heartbeat</code></strong> assigns the kernel heartbeat trigger. Clockwork Bird reports this assignment for the M1, and Raspberry Pi’s overlay reference documents these parameters. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Original LED observation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/"> <a href="https://clockworkbird9.wordpress.com/2023/05/03/sensecap-m1-raspberry-pi-shield/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Original LED observation</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="gpio-led overlay reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux/blob/rpi-6.12.y/arch/arm/boot/dts/overlays/README"> <a href="https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux/blob/rpi-6.12.y/arch/arm/boot/dts/overlays/README" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >gpio-led overlay reference</a> </span> </p> <p>After reboot, inspect the registered LED:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ls -l /sys/class/leds/ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cat /sys/class/leds/lorawan/trigger </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The expected result is a <code>lorawan</code> LED entry with <code>heartbeat</code> selected in brackets. A blinking LED demonstrates this GPIO/driver path. It does not report successful LoRaWAN registration, radio reception, or Helium status.</p> <h2 id="investigate-i2c-devices"> <a href="#investigate-i2c-devices" title="Investigate I2C Devices">Investigate I2C Devices</a> <a href="#investigate-i2c-devices" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Investigate I2C Devices">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An I2C address is a clue, not a device identity.</strong> Clockwork Bird observed responses at <code>0x60</code> and <code>0x39</code>, then read ATECC608 information through the crypto library. The temperature-sensor identification remained tentative in the original article.</p> <p>Start with the adapter listing from the previous section. Broad <code>i2cdetect</code> scans send probing transactions rather than passively observing traffic, and the upstream manual warns about disruption. Avoid routine scans of a running gateway or unknown attached devices. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="i2c-tools probing behavior"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/utils/i2c-tools/i2c-tools/+/refs/tags/v4.3/tools/i2cdetect.8"> <a href="https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/utils/i2c-tools/i2c-tools/+/refs/tags/v4.3/tools/i2cdetect.8" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >i2c-tools probing behavior</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>Supported conclusion</th> <th>Unresolved question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Response at <code>0x60</code></strong></td> <td>Something acknowledged the probe</td> <td>Is it the expected secure element?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Response at <code>0x39</code></strong></td> <td>Something acknowledged the probe</td> <td>Which component and revision responded?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>UU</code> in a scan</strong></td> <td>A driver owns the address and probing was skipped</td> <td>Which driver has ownership?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No response</strong></td> <td>The probe received no acknowledgement</td> <td>Power, bus, ownership, or device protocol?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3 id="a-stronger-temperature-sensor-lead"> <a href="#a-stronger-temperature-sensor-lead" title="A Stronger Temperature-Sensor Lead">A Stronger Temperature-Sensor Lead</a> <a href="#a-stronger-temperature-sensor-lead" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Stronger Temperature-Sensor Lead">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>STTS751 is a source-supported candidate for <code>0x39</code>.</strong> Semtech’s temperature-driver header explicitly associates <code>0x39</code> with <code>STTS751-0DP3F</code>. This strengthens the original hypothesis without identifying every board populated at this address. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Semtech STTS751 driver header"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal/blob/master/libloragw/inc/loragw_stts751.h"> <a href="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal/blob/master/libloragw/inc/loragw_stts751.h" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Semtech STTS751 driver header</a> </span> </p> <p>After identifying a compatible component and ensuring no other process owns it, these commands read its identification registers:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo i2cget <span style="color:#ae81ff">1</span> 0x39 0xfd b </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo i2cget <span style="color:#ae81ff">1</span> 0x39 0xfe b </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Here <strong><code>1</code></strong> selects the verified bus, <strong><code>0x39</code></strong> selects the device, and <strong><code>b</code></strong> requests an SMBus byte-data read. For an STTS751-0, the documented product ID at <code>0xFD</code> is <code>0x00</code>, and the manufacturer ID at <code>0xFE</code> is <code>0x53</code>. These transactions select register addresses but do not program configuration values. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="STTS751 datasheet, register map and identification registers"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/stts751.pdf"> <a href="https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/stts751.pdf" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >STTS751 datasheet, register map and identification registers</a> </span> </p> <p>Compare the readings with the chip marking and documentation. A matching pair adds evidence for identification, while an error calls for checking the bus and ownership before changing hardware configuration. The sensor measures its local temperature, which is a different measurement from the Pi’s CPU temperature.</p> <h2 id="inspect-the-secure-element"> <a href="#inspect-the-secure-element" title="Inspect the Secure Element">Inspect the Secure Element</a> <a href="#inspect-the-secure-element" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Inspect the Secure Element">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The ATECC608 is a separate authentication component.</strong> Treat its configuration, serial number, public key, and protected key material as distinct concepts. A readable public key does not reveal the corresponding private key.</p> <p>Microchip’s <strong>CryptoAuthLib</strong> provides the device interface. Its <strong>cryptoauthtools</strong> repository contains examples built around the library. Prepare the native library and Python bindings for your target system using those projects’ instructions before invoking an example. Installing an unrelated Python package or copying one script alone does not establish an operational I2C backend. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microchip CryptoAuthLib"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthlib"> <a href="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthlib" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microchip CryptoAuthLib</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microchip cryptoauthtools"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthtools"> <a href="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthtools" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microchip cryptoauthtools</a> </span> </p> <p>From a prepared <code>cryptoauthtools/python/examples</code> directory, the original article’s inspection command is:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sudo python3 info.py -i i2c </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The <strong><code>-i i2c</code></strong> argument selects the interface. With a virtual environment, use its explicit Python interpreter and ensure it locates the matching native library. <code>sudo python3</code> selects the system interpreter in many installations, which explains some module-import failures.</p> <p>The reviewed <code>info.py</code> reads revision information, the serial number, configuration, and lock status. For a locked data zone, it attempts to retrieve the public key from slot 0. It does not run the example provisioning sequence. A slot-0 public-key failure alone does not establish a broken device. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microchip info.py source"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthtools/blob/master/python/examples/info.py"> <a href="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthtools/blob/master/python/examples/info.py" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microchip info.py source</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Output or operation</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Configuration locked</strong></td> <td>Configuration restrictions are in force</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data zone locked</strong></td> <td>Interpret access through the configured slot policies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Public key displayed</strong></td> <td>Public information was retrieved, not a private-key export</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>config.py</code> execution</strong></td> <td>Provisioning example with configuration, locking, and key-generation operations</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Do not run <code>config.py</code> to repair an inspection error.</strong> Its source includes configuration writes, zone-locking calls, and key generation. Its default key-generation path also matters on an already configured device. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microchip config.py source"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthtools/blob/master/python/examples/config.py"> <a href="https://github.com/MicrochipTech/cryptoauthtools/blob/master/python/examples/config.py" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microchip config.py source</a> </span> </p> <p>Microchip’s documented provisioning profiles illustrate why a locked data zone does not mean every slot has identical access permissions. Those profiles do not establish the M1’s exact configuration. Preserve the device’s existing configuration and consult the matching part documentation before planning any reuse involving keys. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microchip memory and slot-access policies"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-8F01540E-14A9-479E-9D27-FFFB14DE474E-en-US-2/GUID-92031846-201F-42DA-831D-FA3B6CF79B9B.html"> <a href="https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-8F01540E-14A9-479E-9D27-FFFB14DE474E-en-US-2/GUID-92031846-201F-42DA-831D-FA3B6CF79B9B.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microchip memory and slot-access policies</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="handle-fan-and-button-unknowns"> <a href="#handle-fan-and-button-unknowns" title="Handle Fan and Button Unknowns">Handle Fan and Button Unknowns</a> <a href="#handle-fan-and-button-unknowns" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Handle Fan and Button Unknowns">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A three-pin fan socket does not establish its voltage, polarity, or control method.</strong> Photograph its pin numbering and read the fan label. Resolve power and control connections before attaching a replacement or choosing a GPIO overlay.</p> <p>Likewise, the original investigation leaves the button’s GPIO unknown. Search for a driver or configuration tied to your board revision, then verify connectivity with power disconnected. Do not assign every apparently unused GPIO as an output to find the button.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Peripheral</th> <th>Evidence to collect</th> <th>Acceptance condition</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Fan power</strong></td> <td>Fan rating, connector ground and supply</td> <td>Measured supply matches the fan specification</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fan control</strong></td> <td>Driver/configuration or traced control circuit</td> <td>Defined behavior at startup and elevated temperature</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>User button</strong></td> <td>Contact wiring, GPIO mapping, input polarity</td> <td>One intentional press produces the expected event</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A fresh OS installation does not automatically reproduce the original appliance’s cooling policy. During your first sustained test, observe fan operation and temperatures together. Preserve the enclosure’s airflow path and stop the test if the assembly loses its required cooling.</p> <h2 id="choose-a-gateway-stack"> <a href="#choose-a-gateway-stack" title="Choose a Gateway Stack">Choose a Gateway Stack</a> <a href="#choose-a-gateway-stack" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choose a Gateway Stack">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Separate board support from server protocol.</strong> A compatible LoRaWAN server does not fix an incorrect reset routine or RF calibration. First choose software with support for the concentrator, carrier wiring, OS, and regional configuration.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Software path</th> <th>Useful role</th> <th>Check before deployment</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Semtech SX1302 HAL</strong></td> <td>Source-level bring-up and diagnostic tools</td> <td>Board reset routine and module configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>LoRa Basics Station</strong></td> <td>Authenticated gateway connection to a server</td> <td>Working board integration and server credentials</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ChirpStack Concentratord</strong></td> <td>Dedicated concentrator service</td> <td>Supported model, calibration, and GPIO mapping</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>ChirpStack lists a <strong><code>seeed_wm1302</code></strong> SPI model. This is evidence of module support, not a promise of a complete M1 image or support for every M1 revision. Avoid treating the separate SenseCAP M2 installation instructions as M1 firmware instructions. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="ChirpStack hardware support"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.chirpstack.io/docs/chirpstack-concentratord/hardware-support.html"> <a href="https://www.chirpstack.io/docs/chirpstack-concentratord/hardware-support.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >ChirpStack hardware support</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="ChirpStack’s Seeed installation target"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.chirpstack.io/docs/chirpstack-gateway-os/install/seeed.html"> <a href="https://www.chirpstack.io/docs/chirpstack-gateway-os/install/seeed.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >ChirpStack’s Seeed installation target</a> </span> </p> <p>For The Things Stack, its documentation recommends <strong>LoRa Basics Station</strong> over the legacy Semtech UDP forwarder. Station provides TLS and token-based authentication alongside centralized configuration features. Existing UDP examples are useful for understanding packet forwarding, but their server-address settings do not provide those protections. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="The Things Stack UDP guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/gateways/concepts/udp/"> <a href="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/gateways/concepts/udp/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >The Things Stack UDP guidance</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="LoRa Basics Station documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/gateways/concepts/lora-basics-station/"> <a href="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/gateways/concepts/lora-basics-station/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >LoRa Basics Station documentation</a> </span> </p> <h3 id="prepare-the-upstream-tools"> <a href="#prepare-the-upstream-tools" title="Prepare the Upstream Tools">Prepare the Upstream Tools</a> <a href="#prepare-the-upstream-tools" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prepare the Upstream Tools">#</a> </h3> <p>Build on the target Pi in a new working directory:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>git clone https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal.git </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>cd sx1302_hal </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>git rev-parse HEAD </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>make </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Save the commit identifier with your build output. A completed build establishes compiler compatibility, while the radio still requires the verified reset implementation and correct configuration. Semtech’s documentation explains the role of its HAL and helper programs. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SX1302 HAL build and tool documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal"> <a href="https://github.com/Lora-net/sx1302_hal" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >SX1302 HAL build and tool documentation</a> </span> </p> <p>Review the reset file before running hardware-access tools:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sed -n <span style="color:#e6db74">'1,180p'</span> tools/reset_lgw.sh </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Do not copy this file into the runtime directory unchanged. Semtech documents automatic reset-script use by its hardware-access programs, including tools used during identification. Your review must cover every assigned pin, signal direction, GPIO API, and startup/shutdown state.</p> <p>After completing board verification, use the selected stack’s instructions to read the concentrator EUI and register the gateway. Preserve the module’s calibration and RF settings when adding the server configuration. In Semtech UDP configuration, <code>gateway_ID</code> represents the EUI, while The Things Stack’s console Gateway ID is its human-readable registration identifier. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="The Things Stack gateway configuration"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/gateways/concepts/udp/"> <a href="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/gateways/concepts/udp/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >The Things Stack gateway configuration</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="prove-sensor-delivery"> <a href="#prove-sensor-delivery" title="Prove Sensor Delivery">Prove Sensor Delivery</a> <a href="#prove-sensor-delivery" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prove Sensor Delivery">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Use staged evidence to locate the first failing layer.</strong> A gateway marked online establishes a server connection. Your acceptance test also needs a known sensor, matching frequency plan, and a decoded application payload.</p> <p>The following sequence is a proposed test plan, not measured M1 results:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Checkpoint</th> <th>Evidence to save</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Host ready</strong></td> <td>OS, kernel, power and interface inventory</td> <td>Linux preparation completed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Concentrator responds</strong></td> <td>EUI and successful initialization log</td> <td>Host-to-concentrator communication works</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Radio receives</strong></td> <td>Expected sensor packet and reception metadata</td> <td>The configured receive path works</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Server accepts</strong></td> <td>Gateway event associated with the sensor</td> <td>Forwarding and server routing work</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application decodes</strong></td> <td>Expected measurement and timestamp</td> <td>The application path works</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Reboot recovery</strong></td> <td>Same checks after restart</td> <td>Startup configuration is reproducible</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>For an <strong>OTAA</strong> sensor, also confirm the activation exchange and subsequent uplink. OTAA means over-the-air activation, the join procedure used to establish a session. A received join request alone does not establish a successful join or downlink path. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="The Things Stack activation documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/devices/concepts/abp-vs-otaa/"> <a href="https://www.thethingsindustries.com/docs/hardware/devices/concepts/abp-vs-otaa/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >The Things Stack activation documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Worked diagnosis:</strong> Suppose the gateway connects to its server and reports its EUI, but your sensor never appears. Prioritize the sensor’s transmit configuration, selected receive channels, antenna path, and radio logs. Reprogramming the ATECC608 would not address the missing evidence in this scenario.</p> <p><strong>Second diagnosis:</strong> Suppose a sensor packet appears locally but never reaches the application. Correlate the packet time with gateway and server events, then inspect routing, device registration, and decoding. An RF packet in a log is insufficient evidence for blaming the payload decoder until the server accepts the event.</p> <h2 id="troubleshooting-by-symptom"> <a href="#troubleshooting-by-symptom" title="Troubleshooting by Symptom">Troubleshooting by Symptom</a> <a href="#troubleshooting-by-symptom" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshooting by Symptom">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>Check first</th> <th>Next action</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>No SPI device file</strong></td> <td>Active boot configuration and interface settings</td> <td>Enable the intended interface and reboot</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SPI exists, radio fails</strong></td> <td>Power, seating, reset sequence and chip select</td> <td>Verify the electrical path before server changes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GPIO export error</strong></td> <td>Legacy sysfs assumptions and installed kernel</td> <td>Use a reviewed implementation for the GPIO API</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GPIO already in use</strong></td> <td>Consumer shown by <code>gpioinfo</code></td> <td>Resolve ownership before retrying</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>LED fails after setup</strong></td> <td>Overlay application and GPIO22 conflicts</td> <td>Inspect registered LED devices and reset script</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>I2C device absent</strong></td> <td>Bus number, power and existing ownership</td> <td>Investigate without repeated broad scans</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Crypto library import fails</strong></td> <td>Interpreter, bindings and native library path</td> <td>Fix the software environment</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Public-key read fails</strong></td> <td>Slot policy and earlier successful reads</td> <td>Review configuration without provisioning</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fan does not run</strong></td> <td>Verified supply and cooling-control implementation</td> <td>Restore correct cooling before sustained tests</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Uplinks arrive, join fails</strong></td> <td>Downlink path and regional/device settings</td> <td>Trace the join response and receive windows</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Treat each correction as one experiment. Save the previous configuration, change one variable, repeat the same check, and record whether the expected evidence appeared.</p> <h2 id="create-your-hardware-record"> <a href="#create-your-hardware-record" title="Create Your Hardware Record">Create Your Hardware Record</a> <a href="#create-your-hardware-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Create Your Hardware Record">#</a> </h2> <p>Use this template to turn the investigation into a reproducible handover:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Carrier revision and photographs: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Concentrator model, interface and RF band: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Host model / OS / kernel / GPIO tool version: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Supply / antenna / cooling arrangement: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Verified pin mapping and evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Unresolved nets and excluded features: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Software repository and commit: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Reset implementation and GPIO ownership: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Gateway EUI / server / frequency plan: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Sensor activation and decoded uplink evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Reboot recovery result: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Original-card location and rollback procedure: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Decision exercise:</strong> You have an inexpensive bare carrier with no module label, and a more expensive assembly with readable labels and documented operation. Decide which fits your project after adding the missing Pi, concentrator, antenna, supply, and verification time to the comparison. The stronger choice follows the total cost and evidence required for your intended service, rather than the carrier’s advertised price alone.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> A learning project tolerates unresolved wiring if you have measurement tools and time. A gateway supporting operational sensors needs repeatable startup, cooling, software support, and demonstrated delivery. Record which unresolved condition would stop your deployment.</p> <h2 id="后续步骤"> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" title="后续步骤">后续步骤</a> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="后续步骤">#</a> </h2> <p>Start by completing the hardware record and resolving the reset-script discrepancies. Then bring up one known sensor and save evidence through application decoding before adding more devices.</p> <p><strong>Acceptance record:</strong> save the board revision, module label, radio band, supply measurement, active SPI device, GPIO line names, reset sequence, concentrator log, server connection, and one decoded uplink. Mark every value as observed, documented, or still assumed. Do not treat a successful process start as proof of RF performance or application delivery.</p> <p>If your goal is mesh messaging, first compare the protocol roles in our <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Meshtastic, MeshCore, and Reticulum guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/meshtastic-vs-meshcore-vs-reticulum-comparison-guide/"> <a href="/articles/meshtastic-vs-meshcore-vs-reticulum-comparison-guide/" rel="follow me" >Meshtastic, MeshCore, and Reticulum guide</a> </span> . Sharing LoRa radio technology does not establish firmware compatibility. Consult <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MeshtasticD’s supported-hardware documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://meshtastic.org/docs/meshtasticd/"> <a href="https://meshtastic.org/docs/meshtasticd/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MeshtasticD’s supported-hardware documentation</a> </span> for a messaging deployment instead of treating this LoRaWAN procedure as a Meshtastic conversion.</p> <h2 id="sources-and-image-credits"> <a href="#sources-and-image-credits" title="Sources and Image Credits">Sources and Image Credits</a> <a href="#sources-and-image-credits" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Sources and Image Credits">#</a> </h2> <p>Research checked September 12, 2026. item.title: Flock Safety's Sales Pitch: Warrantless Access to Every Movement
item.category: "Privacy Technology" , "Digital Rights" , "Surveillance" , "Legal Analysis" , "Counter Surveillance"
item.description: Flock Safety does not sell cameras. It sells a subscription to warrantless movement data. Here is how the sales pitch works, how it runs against the Fourth Amendment, and why the fight is about the pitch, not the company.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Flock Safety does not sell cameras.</strong> The company sells a searchable record of where vehicles and people go, delivered to law enforcement as a subscription with no warrant and no delay. Watch the sales pitch instead of the hardware, because the pitch is the constitutional problem.</p> <p><em>The video below traces the argument end to end. It names the product, quotes the Fourth Amendment, walks the relevant court cases, and shows the two contradictory pitches Flock makes to different audiences.</em></p> <p>The source video, <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?</a> </span> from the T-Rex Lab channel, lays out the full case. The write-up below keeps the claims and adds the supporting law.</p> <h2 id="要点"> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" title="要点">要点</a> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="要点">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>The camera is a decoy.</strong> The product is the database, and the camera only feeds it.</li> <li><strong>The Fourth Amendment reaches movement records.</strong> Jones and Carpenter extend protection to continuous location tracking.</li> <li><strong>Flock sells access, not data.</strong> The wording reclassifies a search as a query and a record as an access plan.</li> <li><strong>The pitch changes by audience.</strong> Law enforcement hears “no warrants.” The public hears “small and cautious.”</li> <li><strong>Watch the pitch, not the company.</strong> Every competitor selling warrantless access to private movement is the same fight.</li> </ul> <hr> <h2 id="what-the-company-sells"> <a href="#what-the-company-sells" title="What the Company Sells">What the Company Sells</a> <a href="#what-the-company-sells" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Company Sells">#</a> </h2> <p>Flock enters a market where cameras are already everywhere. Tens of millions of commercial cameras watch storefronts. Doorbell cameras sit on nearly half of American homes. Officers wear body cameras and drive dash cameras, and every phone carries several cameras.</p> <p><strong>Cameras are not scarce, so Flock does not sell cameras.</strong> Access to crime footage is not scarce either: victims hand their recordings straight to departments, and phone video of a crime often lands on social media before an officer asks for it. <strong>Automated license plate readers are not new</strong> either. The technology dates to the 1970s and already runs on the traffic signals maintained by transportation departments.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Flock does not sell</th> <th>Why</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Cameras</strong></td> <td>Commercial, doorbell, body, dash, and phone cameras already cover most public space</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Access to footage</strong></td> <td>Victims and bystanders supply footage directly, and phone video spreads online</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>License plate readers</strong></td> <td>The technology dates to the 1970s and already runs on traffic signals</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The scarce thing is the database.</strong> Flock aggregates plate reads, locations, and timestamps into a searchable record of movement, then sells access to it.
